title: Restoring Senses: Implants, Prostheses and Optogenetic Vision

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Which cells does a cochlear implant bypass, and which neural structure does it stimulate directly?
cards.back: It bypasses damaged hair cells and directly stimulates the auditory nerve.
cards.quote: It skips the damaged hair cells and excites the auditory nerve directly,

cards.front: Why must usable spatial channels in a sensory prosthesis be measured in users rather than counted from its hardware?
cards.back: Detail depends on distinct neural groups in the right map locations. Test what users can distinguish; counting contacts or pixels alone cannot establish that.
cards.quote: A prosthesis can deliver detail only as far as it drives distinct groups of neurons, each in the right place on the brain's map.

cards.front: In cochlear implant frequency maps, higher frequencies are assigned to {{c1::basal}} contacts and lower frequencies to apical contacts.
cards.back: The implant borrows the cochlea's frequency place map.
cards.quote: Clinical maps assign higher frequencies to more basal contacts and lower frequencies to more apical ones,
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: In a cochlear implant, how do a contact and a frequency channel differ?
cards.back: A contact is hardware on the array; a channel is a band of frequency information assigned to a contact.
cards.quote: A contact is a piece of hardware on the array. A channel, here, is a band of frequency information assigned to a contact.
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: How does channel interaction limit independent information in a cochlear implant?
cards.back: Neighbouring electric fields overlap and excite overlapping auditory-nerve populations, so separate contacts need not provide independent frequency channels.
cards.quote: Neighbouring contacts produce overlapping electric fields, called channel interaction, so they excite overlapping groups of neurons,
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: A toy cochlear model treats each stimulated neural region as 1.75 mm wide with sharp edges. Along a 16 mm span, approximately how many non-overlapping regions fit?
cards.back: 16 mm / 1.75 mm = 9.14, or about 9 regions. This illustrates overlap; real fields fade gradually, so it does not predict an individual listener's channel count.
cards.quote: About 16 mm ÷ 1.75 mm ≈ 9, far fewer than 22.
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: A cochlear model's stimulation width was chosen to reproduce an observed channel plateau. Why is that match insufficient, and what independent prediction could test the current-spread explanation?
cards.back: Rule: test a prediction the model was not tuned to. The fitted match only illustrates overlap. Predict continued improvement with added channels when contacts sit closer to the nerve, then test that prediction.
cards.quote: The real test is a prediction the arithmetic was not tuned to.
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: Where are the spiral ganglion cell bodies targeted by a cochlear implant?
cards.back: In the modiolus, the cochlea's central core.
cards.quote: The nerve cell bodies the implant targets, the spiral ganglion, sit in the cochlea's central core, the modiolus.
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: Suppose repositioning a cochlear array brings its contacts closer to auditory-nerve cell bodies. If current spread limits channel separation, what happens as more channels are activated, and why?
cards.back: Useful improvement should extend to more channels: nearer contacts should excite narrower, less overlapping neural groups. This is a prediction, not a guaranteed channel count.
cards.quote: Contacts closer to the nerve should excite narrower groups of neurons, so these listeners should keep improving past 8 to 10 channels.
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: Why can extra cochlear contacts help speech recognition in noise even when a simpler speech test has plateaued?
cards.back: A plateau depends on the task and listener. Overlapping fields can still convey extra information useful under harder conditions; benefit does not prove each contact is independent.
cards.quote: A benefit under hard conditions does not mean each contact is independent, either.
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: An absolute change in a cochlear implant user's percent-correct word score is expressed in {{c1::percentage points}}.
cards.back: An absolute score change differs from a relative percentage change.
cards.quote: mean improvement in CNC word recognition at six months was 40.5 percentage points,
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: In a hypothetical hearing study, a participant's word-recognition score rises from 40% to 60%. Calculate the absolute gain in percentage points and the relative percentage increase from baseline.
cards.back: Absolute gain = 60 − 40 = 20 percentage points. Relative increase = 100 × (60 − 40)/40 = 50%. The relative calculation divides by the baseline score.
cards.quote: mean improvement in CNC word recognition at six months was 40.5 percentage points,
cards.section: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers

cards.front: How can stimulation at one epiretinal electrode produce an elongated percept rather than a dot?
cards.back: Current can recruit passing ganglion-cell axons representing different visual locations. Activating a bundle can therefore evoke a streak; this explanation is model-supported.
cards.quote: Recruiting cells along a bundle of passing axons activates a stretch of visual locations at once,
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: An axon-pathway model accounts for elongated percept drawings from four retinal-implant users. A report calls this direct evidence that the passing axons fired. Is that justified?
cards.back: No. The drawings and model support an axon-of-passage explanation, but they are not direct recordings of those axons.
cards.quote: That is a model-supported explanation of the drawings, not a direct recording of the axons.
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: PRIMA's subretinal photovoltaic pixels convert near-infrared light into current that stimulates {{c1::bipolar cells}}.
cards.back: Signals then pass through the surviving inner retinal network to ganglion cells.
cards.quote: convert that light into current that stimulates bipolar cells, the first surviving inner retinal neurons,
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: Why is a local return electrode around each PRIMA pixel expected to improve spatial selectivity?
cards.back: Current flows out and back within a small area, which is meant to confine the field. This is a design argument, not proof of superiority.
cards.quote: current flows out and back within a small area instead of spreading toward a distant return,
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: What does logMAR measure, and does a higher value mean finer or worse acuity?
cards.back: The base-10 logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution in arcminutes. Higher values mean worse acuity.
cards.quote: A logMAR of 0 is 20/20, 1.0 is 20/200, and higher is worse.
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: For a 100 µm retinal pixel, assume 288 µm per degree and a minimum resolvable detail one pixel wide. Convert its nominal limit to arcminutes, logMAR and Snellen acuity; use denominator = 20 × 10^logMAR.
cards.back: (100/288)° × 60 ≈ 20.8 arcmin; log10(20.8) ≈ 1.32. The denominator is 20 × (100/288) × 60 ≈ 416.7, or about 20/420. This assumes separate pixel channels, not guaranteed performance.
cards.quote: That is an ideal sampling estimate, not a guaranteed score.
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: A hypothetical retinal chip halves pixels from 100 µm to 50 µm, but each stimulation field still spans 100 µm. Using 288 µm per degree and Snellen denominator = 20 × detail in arcminutes, calculate the nominal new pixel estimate. Does it establish twice the spatial detail?
cards.back: Nominal: 20 × (50/288) × 60 = 208.3, about 20/210. Rule: usable detail requires distinct neural groups. Each field spans 2 pixel widths; overlap breaks the independent-pixel assumption, so finer hardware does not guarantee twice the detail.
cards.quote: If each pixel's field stays within that pixel and each pixel acts as a separate channel,
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: PRIMAvera's mean native acuity matched the nominal pixel estimate near 1.32 logMAR. Does this prove that every pixel drives a separate neural population?
cards.back: No. The pixel estimate assumes separate channels, and retinal scale varies between eyes. Agreement of a trial mean with that estimate supports the design aim but does not prove confinement of every field.
cards.quote: It fits what the design aims for, pixels that act as separate channels, but one trial's mean does not prove that each field is confined.
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: Why should a visual implant's acuity with adjustable zoom be reported separately from its native resolution?
cards.back: Zoom-assisted performance measures the implant plus magnification. It can improve chart scores without adding pixels, so it does not isolate native implant resolution.
cards.quote: A zoom-assisted chart score measures the implant plus a magnifier, not extra pixels.
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: Argus II's best reported grating acuity was about 20/1260, finer than an ideal static-grid spacing estimate near 20/2400. What assumption about the estimate should be rejected?
cards.back: Reject treating the nominal spacing estimate as a hard performance limit. Camera mapping, test choice and distorted percepts can change real scores.
cards.quote: A conversion like this is a nominal estimate, not a hard limit:
cards.section: Why a retinal electrode does not make a pixel

cards.front: In optogenetic therapy, a viral vector makes surviving cells express a {{c1::light-sensitive protein}}.
cards.back: The cells are changed to respond to light.
cards.quote: In an optogenetic therapy, a viral vector makes surviving cells express a light-sensitive protein;
cards.section: Putting the signal in with light instead of current

cards.front: Why did the ChrimsonR vision approach require stimulating goggles rather than relying on ordinary room light?
cards.back: ChrimsonR needs much brighter light than photoreceptors do; ordinary room light does not drive it. The goggles provide activating amber-light pulses.
cards.quote: Microbial light sensors such as ChrimsonR need far brighter light than photoreceptors do, so ordinary room light does not drive them.
cards.section: Putting the signal in with light instead of current

cards.front: Why must goggles perform some scene encoding when optogenetic stimulation directly targets retinal ganglion cells?
cards.back: Direct stimulation of retinal output cells skips processing normally performed by bipolar and amacrine cells, so the goggles must supply part of that encoding.
cards.quote: driving the retina's output cells directly skips the processing that bipolar and amacrine cells would normally do,
cards.section: Putting the signal in with light instead of current

cards.front: After ChrimsonR treatment, a patient locates objects with the stimulating goggles but detects none without them. What dependence does that comparison establish, and within what scope?
cards.back: The response depended on goggle light in that patient and those tasks. It does not establish normal vision or how often the therapy succeeds in others.
cards.quote: it shows that, in this patient and in these tasks, the response depended on the goggle light.
cards.section: Putting the signal in with light instead of current

cards.front: A team claims its light-based vision therapy has more usable spatial channels than a retinal chip because users can locate objects. The chip study measured acuity. What evidence is missing?
cards.back: Measure comparable spatial discrimination. Rule: usable channels depend on what users can distinguish; successful object localization alone does not count separately addressable places or support a ranking against an acuity result.
cards.quote: The results in this lesson are object tasks and light sensitivity, not acuity, so they do not say how many separate places this approach can address.
cards.section: Putting the signal in with light instead of current

cards.front: The hand region where a sensation is felt during somatosensory cortical electrode stimulation is its {{c1::projected field}}.
cards.back: It is an approximate address; fields can overlap or change with the stimulus.
cards.quote: Stimulating an electrode evoked a sensation felt in a region of the hand, its projected field.
cards.section: Writing touch: addresses, then patterns

cards.front: How can a cortical touch interface vary the felt strength of stimulation at one electrode?
cards.back: Changing stimulation amplitude grades perceived intensity, so felt strength can be adjusted through stimulation at that electrode.
cards.why: Projected fields can overlap and change with the stimulus, so intensity control does not guarantee an unchanged location.
cards.quote: Changing the amplitude graded the perceived intensity, and many percepts remained stable for months.
cards.section: Writing touch: addresses, then patterns

cards.front: What did reports of natural-feeling phantom-hand sensations from peripheral nerve cuffs establish about normal touch?
cards.back: They supported repeatable, useful artificial sensations in the tested participants. Two participants and subjective naturalness ratings did not establish normal touch.
cards.quote: Two participants and subjective ratings do not establish normal touch.
cards.section: Writing touch: addresses, then patterns

cards.front: In a robotic-arm study, one participant's median task time changed from 20.9 s without touch feedback to 10.2 s with it. Calculate the absolute and baseline-relative percentage reduction.
cards.back: 20.9 − 10.2 = 10.7 s. Relative reduction = 100 × 10.7/20.9 = 51.2%. These compare two medians from one participant, not a mean paired effect or a population effect.
cards.quote: It is not a mean paired effect and not a population effect.
cards.section: Writing touch: addresses, then patterns

cards.front: A tactile-feedback study repeats many sessions in one participant, then treats each session as an independent person when estimating a population effect. What design change addresses the problem, and why?
cards.back: Recruit independent participants. Rule: repeated trials in one person are not independent replicates. More sessions can characterize that person's performance but cannot substitute for sampling other people.
cards.quote: Repeated trials in one person are not independent replicates.
cards.section: Writing touch: addresses, then patterns

cards.front: A cortical touch interface changes from stimulating separate hand locations to a sequence of stimulation across locations and time. What new percept could become possible, and why?
cards.back: Apparent motion with controllable direction and speed could become possible, because spatiotemporal patterns encode more than isolated locations. This does not imply restoration of every touch quality.
cards.quote: spatiotemporal patterns evoked apparent motion with controllable speed and direction.
cards.section: Writing touch: addresses, then patterns

cards.front: Reproducing task-relevant features of a natural neural code as a sensory-prosthesis design strategy is called {{c1::biomimicry}}.
cards.back: Test the resulting percept and behaviour.
cards.quote: biomimicry: reproduce the task-relevant features of the natural neural code, then test the percept and the behaviour.
cards.section: The second half: sending the right pattern

cards.front: How does the simple biomimetic cortical-touch pulse scheme emphasize contact onset and offset?
cards.back: Pulse amplitude changes over the contact to approximate stronger activity at onset and offset, while pulse rate stays fixed.
cards.quote: In the simple scheme the pulse amplitude changes over the contact while the pulse rate stays fixed;
cards.section: The second half: sending the right pattern

cards.front: Biomimetic touch stimulation improved naturalness on 32% of tested single electrodes and 75% of tested four-electrode groups. Can those percentages alone establish a controlled head-to-head advantage of the advanced scheme?
cards.back: No. The denominators differ: individual electrodes versus electrode groups. These are not directly comparable fractions from a controlled head-to-head test.
cards.quote: The denominators differ (electrodes against electrode groups), so the two percentages are not a controlled head-to-head comparison.
cards.section: The second half: sending the right pattern

cards.front: A hypothetical natural-code touch pattern feels more natural and needs less charge than a constant pulse train. What additional experiment would test whether it improves prosthesis control?
cards.back: Compare task performance under the natural-code and control patterns. Rule: biomimicry calls for testing both percept and behaviour; better naturalness or lower charge alone does not establish better control or prove that closer imitation always improves performance.
cards.quote: reproduce the task-relevant features of the natural neural code, then test the percept and the behaviour.
cards.section: The second half: sending the right pattern

cards.front: Why can a single-arm visual-implant trial not isolate improvement caused by the device itself?
cards.back: Surgery, device use, training and time change together. Without a comparison group, improvement cannot be separated from practice and time.
cards.quote: surgery, device use, training and time all change together.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: At twelve months, 26 of 32 assessed PRIMAvera participants met the ≥0.2 logMAR improvement endpoint with zoom allowed; 38 were implanted. Calculate assessed-only and all-implanted rates, counting all six missing as nonresponders. How does the reported 80% imputation estimate differ?
cards.back: Assessed: 100 × 26/32 = 81.3%. All implanted with missing treated as failures: 100 × 26/38 = 68.4%. The 80% estimate instead statistically fills in missing outcomes using assumptions; it is a third result.
cards.quote: The multiple-imputation estimate of 80 percent is a third number, built on assumptions about the missing six.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: PRIMAvera reported 26 serious device- or procedure-related events in 19 participants. Why must both counts appear beside the benefit?
cards.back: Events and affected people are different counts: some participants can have multiple events. Reporting both preserves the safety burden rather than treating 26 events as 26 people.
cards.quote: Nineteen participants had 26 serious device- or procedure-related events over the twelve months,
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How would you redesign a single-arm visual-implant study to separate improvement from practice and time?
cards.back: Include an untreated or deferred-implantation comparison group, masked acuity assessors where feasible, and a prespecified endpoint. Rule: surgery, device use, training and time co-vary in a single arm; a comparison helps distinguish improvement from practice and time.
cards.quote: A comparison group, such as an untreated or deferred-implantation group, so the change can be separated from practice and time.
cards.section: Design problem
